claim: Acanthurus triostegus crest captured individuals experience an important weight loss between day 1 (0.71 ± 0.01 g) and day 8 (0.53 ± 0.01 g) following their entry in the reef.
source: A. triostegus crest captured individuals (n = 297) experience an important weight loss between day 1 (0.71 ± 0.01 g) and day 8 (0.53 ± 0.01 g) following their entry in the reef (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements of weight at different time points and presented in Figure 1B.

claim: Acanthurus triostegus individuals undergo extensive pigmentation changes during larval recruitment, including the very rapid appearance of black stripes (less than four hours) after entering the reef.
source: Individuals also undergo extensive pigmentation changes (Figure 1C–L), as exemplified by the very rapid appearance of black stripes (less than four hours, MB pers. obs.) after entering the reef (Figure 1C–D, H-I).
evidence: Supported by observational data and visual documentation in Figure 1C-L.

claim: Three different dental generations (A, B, and C) are present in Acanthurus triostegus from crest larvae to day 8 juveniles.
source: Furthermore, using conventional X-Ray microtomography, we identified three different dental generations in crest larvae to day 8 juveniles (red, blue and green, Figure 1M–Q).
evidence: Supported by X-ray microtomography imaging data shown in Figure 1M-Q.

claim: Crest larvae already have teeth of the C dentition about to erupt, indicating that fish are prepared for reef life conditions before reef entry.
source: The fact that crest captured larvae already have teeth of the C dentition about to erupt (Figure 1M) indicates that fish are prepared for reef life conditions before reef entry.
evidence: Based on inference from X-ray microtomography data showing developing dentition C in crest larvae.

claim: The gastro-intestinal tract of Acanthurus triostegus lengthens from about 2.52 ± 0.07 cm in crest captured larvae to 7.38 ± 0.14 cm in day 8 juveniles.
source: In particular, the gastro-intestinal tract lengthens from about 2.52 ± 0.07 cm in crest captured larvae to 7.38 ± 0.14 cm in day 8 juveniles (Figure 1W).
evidence: Supported by direct measurements of intestine length presented in Figure 1W.

claim: At day 3, intestines of Acanthurus triostegus undergo a spectacular remodeling with the disappearance of the epithelium, leaving only the muscular layer.
source: At day 3, intestines undergo a spectacular remodeling with the disappearance of the epithelium, leaving only the muscular layer (Figure 1T), while epithelium reformation occurs later at day 5 (Figure 1U).
evidence: Supported by histological section data shown in Figure 1T and 1U.

claim: T4 levels are low in far ocean larvae and rise in fish located closer to the reef (near ocean larvae), before dropping 6-fold between the near ocean larvae and the day 8 juveniles.
source: T4 levels are low in far ocean larvae and rise in fish located closer to the reef (near ocean larvae), before dropping 6-fold between the near ocean larvae and the day 8 juveniles (p-value=0.001, Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by T4 hormone measurements at different developmental stages and locations, with statistical significance.

claim: Near ocean and crest captured larvae have similar levels of T3 that are 6-fold higher than the level observed in day 8 juveniles.
source: Near ocean and crest captured larvae have similar levels of T3 that are 6-fold higher than the level observed in day 8 juveniles (p-value < 0.001 Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by T3 hormone measurements with statistical significance shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The three thyroid hormone receptors of Acanthurus triostegus (TRα-A, TRα-B and TRβ) have between 86% and 96% sequence identity with their zebrafish orthologs.
source: These receptors have between 86% (TRα-A) and 96% (TRβ) sequence identity with their zebrafish orthologs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by sequence comparison data presented in supplementary figure.

claim: Transactivation assays show that the three Acanthurus triostegus receptors (TRα-A, TRα-B, TRβ) behave as genuine thyroid hormone receptors.
source: Moreover, transactivation assays show that these receptors behave as genuine TR (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There is a drop of all TR expression between crest larvae and day 8 juveniles in Acanthurus triostegus.
source: We observed a drop of all TR expression between crest larvae and day 8 juveniles (p-values=0.001, 0.005 and 0.002 for TRα-A, TRα-B and TRβ respectively, Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by qPCR gene expression data with statistical significance shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Relocating crest-captured larvae back to the external slope delays the appearance of white pigmentation between the vertical black stripes at day 2 compared to lagoon raised counterparts.
source: Similar to this earlier study, we observed a striking delay in the white pigmentation appearance between the vertical black stripes in day 2 relocated fish compared to their lagoon raised counterparts (Figure 3A, lower panel).
evidence: Supported by observational data and visual comparison shown in Figure 3A, and references earlier study by McCormick, 1999.

claim: The levels of T4 and T3 in fish relocated on the external slope at day 2, day 5 and day 8 are overall higher than the levels of their control counterparts in the lagoon.
source: The levels of T4 and T3 in fish relocated on the external slope at day 2, day 5 and day 8 are overall higher than the levels of their control counterparts in the lagoon (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: Supported by hormone measurement data comparing relocated and control fish shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: The environment effectively controls the metamorphosis by modulating the TH signaling in Acanthurus triostegus.
source: This suggests that the environment effectively controls the metamorphosis by modulating the TH signaling.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that relocated fish maintain higher TH levels and TR expression compared to lagoon fish.

claim: T3 + IOP treatment increases the length of the intestine in day 2 and day 5 juveniles.
source: T3 + IOP treatment increases the length of the intestine in day 2 and day 5 juveniles (p-values<0.001, Figure 3E, blue).
evidence: Supported by experimental treatment data with statistical significance shown in Figure 3E.

claim: NH3 treatment partially prevents the intestines lengthening occurring after recruitment in Acanthurus triostegus.
source: On the contrary, NH3 treatment partially prevents the intestines lengthening occurring after recruitment (p-values<0.001, Figure 3E, green).
evidence: Supported by experimental treatment data with statistical significance shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Intestines of fish relocated on the external slope are shorter than those of their lagoon counterparts at day 2 and day 5.
source: In parallel, intestines of fish relocated on the external slope are shorter than those of their lagoon counterparts at day 2 and day 5 (p-value<0.001 and p-value=0.042 respectively, Figure 3E, orange).
evidence: Supported by experimental relocation data with statistical significance shown in Figure 3E.

claim: T3 + IOP treatment accelerates the loss of the intestinal microvilli at day 2 and accelerates the development and thickening of a new epithelium at day 5.
source: In the anterior part of the guts, while T3 + IOP treatment accelerates the loss of the intestinal microvilli at day 2 and accelerates the development and the thickening of a new epithelium at day 5 (Figure 3F, second column), NH3 treatment and external slope relocation prevent microvilli renewal at both day 2 and day 5 (Figure 3F, third and fourth column).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: NH3 treatment and external slope relocation prevent microvilli renewal at both day 2 and day 5 in Acanthurus triostegus.
source: In the anterior part of the guts, while T3 + IOP treatment accelerates the loss of the intestinal microvilli at day 2 and accelerates the development and the thickening of a new epithelium at day 5 (Figure 3F, second column), NH3 treatment and external slope relocation prevent microvilli renewal at both day 2 and day 5 (Figure 3F, third and fourth column).
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: No effect on teeth development was observed with T3 + IOP or NH3 treatment, nor with external slope relocation.
source: We did not observe any effect on teeth development neither with T3 + IOP or NH3 treatment, nor with external slope relocation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by X-ray microtomography data shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Teeth remodeling is a lengthy process that starts very early on in oceanic larvae and therefore before reef colonization.
source: Given that teeth remodeling is a lengthy process that starts very early on in oceanic larvae and therefore before reef colonization, it is not surprising that the treatments performed on crest captured larvae do not affect (or are too late to affect) teeth development.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that treatments starting at crest capture do not affect teeth development.

claim: T3 + IOP treatment increases the grazing activity by around 50% in day 5 juveniles when compared to the control individuals.
source: T3 + IOP treatment increases the grazing activity by around 50% in day 5 juveniles when compared to the control individuals (p-value=0.004, Figure 3G, blue lanes).
evidence: Supported by behavioral observation data with statistical significance shown in Figure 3G.

claim: NH3 treatment significantly decreases the number of bites at day 2 by 33% in Acanthurus triostegus.
source: On the contrary, NH3 treatment significantly decreases the number of bites at day 2 by 33% (p-value<0.001, Figure 3G, green lane).
evidence: Supported by behavioral observation data with statistical significance shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The grazing activity of fish relocated on the external slope is diminished by more than 4-fold at day 2.
source: The grazing activity of fish relocated on the external slope (Figure 3A) is also diminished by more than 4-fold at day 2 (p-value<0.001, Figure 3G, orange lanes).
evidence: Supported by behavioral observation data with statistical significance shown in Figure 3G.

claim: TH signaling promotes the biting activity of Acanthurus triostegus and subsequent grazing behavior adopted at larval recruitment.
source: These data indicate that TH signaling promotes the biting activity of A. triostegus and subsequent grazing behavior adopted at larval recruitment.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing that TH agonist increases and TH antagonist decreases grazing activity.

claim: TH controls the transformations of the feeding process in Acanthurus triostegus not only at the morphological and physiological levels but also at the behavioral level.
source: This shows that TH controls the transformations of the feeding process not only at the morphological and physiological levels but also at the behavioral level.
evidence: Inferred from combined data on intestine morphology, physiology, and grazing behavior in response to TH manipulation.

claim: In four coral fish species (Rhinecanthus aculeatus, Chromis viridis, Chaetodon lunula and Ostorhinchus angustatus), both T4 and T3 levels drop between day 1 and day 8.
source: In these species, both T4 and T3 levels drop between day 1 and day 8, up to 3-fold for T4 (in O. angustatus, p-value=0.029) and up to 4-fold for T3 (in R. aculeatus, p-value=0.05) (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by hormone measurements in four different species with statistical significance shown in Figure 4.

claim: The drop of TH levels after reef entry strongly suggests that TH are key determinants for the metamorphosis of Rhinecanthus aculeatus, Chromis viridis, Chaetodon lunula and Ostorhinchus angustatus.
source: This drop of TH levels after reef entry strongly suggests that TH are also key determinants for the metamorphosis of these species.
evidence: Inferred from the pattern of TH levels dropping after reef entry in multiple species.

claim: T4 levels in Rhinecanthus aculeatus and T3 levels in Chromis viridis rise between near ocean and day 1 individuals.
source: T4 levels in R. aculeatus and T3 levels in C. viridis also rise between near ocean and day 1 individuals (Figure 4), further confirming the model of a TH-mediated metamorphosis during coral reef fish larval recruitment.
evidence: Supported by hormone measurement data shown in Figure 4 and used to support the TH-mediated metamorphosis model.

claim: CPF treatment at 30 µg.l−1 decreases the T3 levels by 50% in day 2 juveniles of Acanthurus triostegus.
source: CPF treatment at 30 µg.l−1 decreases the T3 levels by 50% in day 2 juveniles (p-value=0.021, Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by hormone measurement data with statistical significance shown in Figure 5A.

claim: No significant effect of CPF was observed on T4 levels regardless of CPF concentration and duration.
source: No significant effect was observed on T4 levels regardless of CPF concentration and duration (p-value=0.205 for day 2 and p-value=0.496 for day 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by hormone measurement data with statistical analysis shown in supplementary figure.

claim: CPF exposure at 30 µg.l−1 prevents guts' lengthening at day 2 in Acanthurus triostegus.
source: However, CPF exposure at 30 µg.l−1 prevents guts' lengthening at day 2 (p-value=0.024, Figure 5B left panel), and both exposure at 5 and 30 µg.l−1 prevent intestines' lengthening at day 5 (p-values=0.047 and 0.029 respectively, Figure 5B right panel).
evidence: Supported by intestine length measurement data with statistical significance shown in Figure 5B.

claim: CPF exposure at 5 and 30 µg.l−1 prevents intestines' lengthening at day 5 in Acanthurus triostegus.
source: However, CPF exposure at 30 µg.l−1 prevents guts' lengthening at day 2 (p-value=0.024, Figure 5B left panel), and both exposure at 5 and 30 µg.l−1 prevent intestines' lengthening at day 5 (p-values=0.047 and 0.029 respectively, Figure 5B right panel).
evidence: Supported by intestine length measurement data with statistical significance shown in Figure 5B.

claim: CPF exposure at 30 µg.l−1 decreases the grazing activity of day 2 juveniles with 2.63 ± 0.09 bites per fish per min contrasting with 3.62 ± 0.28 bites per fish per min in the solvent control condition.
source: Strikingly, CPF exposure at 30 µg.l−1 also decreases the grazing activity of day 2 juveniles with 2.63 ± 0.09 bites per fish per min contrasting with 3.62 ± 0.28 bites per fish per min in the solvent control condition (p-value=0.014, Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by behavioral observation data with statistical significance shown in Figure 5C.

claim: CPF exposure at 5 and 30 µg.l−1 decreases the grazing activity in day 5 juveniles with respectively 2.68 ± 0.18 and 2.63 ± 0.05 bites per fish per min compared to 4.43 ± 0.33 bites per fish per min for the solvent control fish.
source: In day 5 juveniles, exposure at 5 and 30 µg.l−1 decreases the grazing activity with respectively 2.68 ± 0.18 and 2.63 ± 0.05 bites per fish per min compared to 4.43 ± 0.33 bites per fish per min for the solvent control fish (p-values=0.001, Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by behavioral observation data with statistical significance shown in Figure 5C.

claim: CPF treatment results in up to a 14-fold reduction in the biomass of turf grazed after 5 days.
source: Such a behavior in fish treated with CPF results in up to a 14-fold reduction in the biomass of turf grazed after 5 days (p-value=0.05, Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by measurement of grazed algae biomass with statistical significance shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Larval recruitment, the transition of pelagic larvae into reef-associated juveniles, is a critical step for the resilience of marine fish populations.
source: Larval recruitment, the transition of pelagic larvae into reef-associated juveniles, is a critical step for the resilience of marine fish populations but its molecular control is unknown.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Chlorpyrifos is a pesticide often encountered in coral-reefs.
source: Likewise, chlorpyrifos, a pesticide often encountered in coral-reefs, impairs A. triostegus TH-levels, transformation, and grazing activity, hence diminishing this herbivore's ability to control the spread of reef-algae.
evidence: Stated as known fact and supported by citations to Roche et al., 2011 and Botté et al., 2012 in the introduction.

claim: Life history transitions are critical for many animal species and often correspond to concomitant developmental and ecological shifts.
source: Life history transitions are critical for many animal species and often correspond to concomitant developmental and ecological shifts (Bishop et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bishop et al., 2006.

claim: The life cycle of most teleost reef fish include a major developmental and ecological transition where adults reproduce in the vicinity of the reef, emitting eggs that disperse and hatch in the ocean, where the larvae grow.
source: The life cycle of most teleost reef fish include a major developmental and ecological transition. Adults reproduce in the vicinity of the reef, emitting eggs that disperse and hatch in the ocean, where the larvae grow (Leis and McCormick, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Leis and McCormick, 2002.

claim: Larvae migrate back and enter reefs where they become juveniles, a step called larval recruitment.
source: Larvae migrate back and enter reefs where they become juveniles, a step called larval recruitment (Leis and McCormick, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Leis and McCormick, 2002.

claim: Larval recruitment involves the perception of environmental cues for larvae to localize and settle in the reef, and is accompanied by major morphological changes.
source: This step involves the perception of environmental cues for larvae to localize and settle in the reef, and is accompanied by major morphological changes (McCormick et al., 2002; Lecchini et al., 2005b, 2005a; Lecchini et al., 2013; Barth, 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to McCormick et al., 2002; Lecchini et al., 2005b, 2005a; Lecchini et al., 2013; Barth, 2015.

claim: The transition of pelagic larvae into reef-associated juveniles is often referred to as metamorphosis and is critical for the maintenance of reef fish populations, but its molecular control remains largely unknown.
source: This transition of pelagic larvae into reef-associated juveniles is often referred to as metamorphosis and is critical for the maintenance of reef fish populations, but its molecular control remains largely unknown (Dufour and Galzin, 1993; Doherty, 2002; Leis and McCormick, 2002; McCormick et al., 2002; Dixson et al., 2011; Barth, 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to Dufour and Galzin, 1993; Doherty, 2002; Leis and McCormick, 2002; McCormick et al., 2002; Dixson et al., 2011; Barth, 2015.

claim: TH and their receptors (TR) trigger and coordinate metamorphosis of many species such as Xenopus or flatfish.
source: TH and their receptors (TR) trigger and coordinate metamorphosis of many species such as Xenopus (Brown and Cai, 2007) or flatfish (Solbakken et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brown and Cai, 2007 and Solbakken et al., 1999.

claim: The thyroid gland produces mainly the thyroxine hormone (T4), which is peripherally transformed into triiodothyronine (T3), the active form.
source: The thyroid gland produces mainly the thyroxine hormone (T4), which is peripherally transformed into triiodothyronine (T3), the active form (Chopra, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chopra, 1996.

claim: The transformation of T4 into T3, and the degradation of T4 and T3 are controlled by a family of enzymes called deiodinases.
source: The transformation of T4 into T3, and the degradation of T4 and T3 are controlled by a family of enzymes called deiodinases (Bianco and Kim, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bianco and Kim, 2006.

claim: TH levels peak at the climax of metamorphosis.
source: TH levels peak at the climax of metamorphosis.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about metamorphosis.

claim: Precocious treatment with TH triggers metamorphosis whereas goitrogen (TH synthesis inhibitors) treatment blocks it.
source: Precocious treatment with TH triggers metamorphosis whereas goitrogen (TH synthesis inhibitors) treatment blocks it (Tata, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tata, 2006.

claim: Similar mechanisms of TH-controlled metamorphosis have been described in several teleost fishes, but in contexts disconnected from the natural environment.
source: Similar mechanisms have been described in several teleost fishes, but in contexts disconnected from the natural environment (Brown, 1997; de Jesus et al., 1998; Yamano and Miwa, 1998; Kawakami et al., 2003; Marchand et al., 2004; McMenamin and Parichy, 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to Brown, 1997; de Jesus et al., 1998; Yamano and Miwa, 1998; Kawakami et al., 2003; Marchand et al., 2004; McMenamin and Parichy, 2013.

claim: In the convict surgeonfish Acanthurus triostegus, larvae have a planktonic diet while juveniles and adults are herbivorous.
source: In the convict surgeonfish Acanthurus triostegus, larvae have a planktonic diet while juveniles and adults are herbivorous, and external morphological changes occurring at recruitment have been previously described (Randall, 1961; McCormick, 1999; McCormick et al., 2002; Frédérich et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Randall, 1961; McCormick, 1999; McCormick et al., 2002; Frédérich et al., 2012.

claim: Crest-captured Acanthurus triostegus larvae can delay their metamorphosis when relocated to the external slope of the reef (open ocean), showing an influence of the environment on their morphological transformation.
source: Interestingly, crest-captured larvae can delay their metamorphosis when relocated to the external slope of the reef (open ocean), showing an influence of the environment on their morphological transformation (McCormick, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to McCormick, 1999.

claim: Acanthurus triostegus larval recruitment to the reefs corresponds to metamorphosis with major pigmentation changes, remodeling of the digestive tract and behavioral modifications.
source: Here we report that A. triostegus larval recruitment to the reefs corresponds to metamorphosis with major pigmentation changes, remodeling of the digestive tract and behavioral modifications.
evidence: Summary statement of the study's findings based on experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: TH levels and TR expressions control the remodeling process during Acanthurus triostegus larval recruitment.
source: Our results show that TH levels and TR expressions control this remodeling process.
evidence: Summary statement of the study's findings based on experimental data on TH levels, TR expression, and manipulation experiments.

claim: Recruiting Acanthurus triostegus larvae can freeze their TH signaling when relocated on the external slope, demonstrating an influence of the environment on metamorphosis.
source: Furthermore, recruiting larvae can freeze their TH signaling when relocated on the external slope, demonstrating an influence of the environment on metamorphosis.
evidence: Summary statement of the study's findings based on experimental data from relocation experiments.

claim: Chlorpyrifos affects Acanthurus triostegus metamorphosis by impairing TH signaling, preventing intestine lengthening, and inhibiting fish grazing activity.
source: Chlorpyrifos (CPF), a known reef pollutant and endocrine disruptor (Roche et al., 2011; Botté et al., 2012; Juberg et al., 2013; Slotkin et al., 2013), affects A. triostegus metamorphosis by impairing TH signaling, preventing intestine lengthening, and inhibiting fish grazing activity.
evidence: Summary statement of the study's findings based on CPF exposure experiments, with citations supporting CPF as a known pollutant and endocrine disruptor.

claim: CPF impairs Acanthurus triostegus control on algae spreading, which is a major threat for reef conservation.
source: CPF therefore impairs A. triostegus control on algae spreading, which is a major threat for reef conservation.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing CPF reduces grazing activity and algae removal, combined with knowledge about algae as a reef threat.

claim: The differences in 16S gut content are likely the consequence of a diet shift (carnivorous to herbivorous) and an environmental shift occurring during larval recruitment.
source: In particular, the differences in 16S gut content are likely the consequence of a diet shift (carnivorous to herbivorous) and an environmental shift occurring during larval recruitment (Frédérich et al., 2012; Baldo et al., 2015; Sullam et al., 2012).
evidence: Inferred from 16S sequencing data and supported by citations to Frédérich et al., 2012; Baldo et al., 2015; Sullam et al., 2012.

claim: Intestine remodeling (i.e. the loss of the villi and internal structures) accelerates the shift of the gut microbiota by allowing the establishment of a new bacterial community fitting the diet change.
source: We hypothesize that intestine remodeling (i.e. the loss of the villi and internal structures) accelerates the shift of the gut microbiota by allowing the establishment of a new bacterial community fitting the diet change.
evidence: Explicitly stated as a hypothesis based on observed intestine remodeling and microbiota changes.

claim: The presence of Lachnospiraceae in the adult but not in the larvae is consistent with the hypothesis that this family of bacteria is acquired through the environment in surgeonfishes.
source: The presence of Lachnospiraceae in the adult but not in the larvae is consistent with the hypothesis that this family of bacteria is acquired through the environment in surgeonfishes (Miyake et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on 16S sequencing data and supported by citation to Miyake et al., 2016.

claim: The fish bacterial community depends on their diet and environment.
source: Altogether, these observations reinforce the notion that the fish bacterial community depends on their diet and environment.
evidence: Inferred from combined observations of diet changes, environmental changes, and microbiota shifts.

claim: The shifts of 16S and 18S gut contents, occurring between crest individuals and day 8 juveniles, strikingly coordinate with both the changes of the intestine and teeth morphologies observed during larval recruitment.
source: These shifts of 16S and 18S gut contents, occurring between crest individuals and day 8 juveniles, strikingly coordinate with both the changes of the intestine and teeth morphologies observed during larval recruitment (Figure 1M–V).
evidence: Based on coordinated observations of gut content changes and morphological changes shown in Figure 1M-V.

claim: All the changes from teeth to microbiota are consistent with Acanthurus triostegus change of diet after entering the reefs.
source: All these changes from teeth to microbiota are consistent with A. triostegus change of diet after entering the reefs, conforming to previous observations (Randall, 1961; McCormick, 1999; Frédérich et al., 2012).
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence (teeth, intestine, microbiota) and supported by citations to Randall, 1961; McCormick, 1999; Frédérich et al., 2012.

claim: The complete remodeling during larval recruitment is associated with a severe weight loss, suggesting that larval recruitment corresponds to a real metabolic challenge.
source: This complete remodeling is associated with a severe weight loss (Figure 1B), suggesting that larval recruitment corresponds to a real metabolic challenge.
evidence: Inferred from observed weight loss data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Migration towards the reefs marks the onset of metamorphosis and starts very early on in Acanthurus triostegus.
source: This indicates that migration towards the reefs marks the onset of metamorphosis and starts very early on (Figure 6A).
evidence: Inferred from TH and TR expression data showing elevated levels in near ocean and crest larvae.

claim: The transformation process is already well advanced when larvae reach the reef, suggesting that this event is triggered in the open ocean by, yet unknown, environmental cues.
source: Consequently, the transformation process is already well advanced when larvae reach the reef, suggesting that this event is triggered in the open ocean by, yet unknown, environmental cues (Figure 6A).
evidence: Inferred from observations that crest larvae already have developing adult dentition and elevated TH levels.

claim: After reef entry, T3 treatment increases gut length while external slope relocation and NH3 treatment delay the metamorphosis, although they could not completely interrupt it.
source: After reef entry, T3 treatment increases gut length while external slope relocation and NH3 treatment delay the metamorphosis, although they could not completely interrupt it (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: Based on experimental manipulation data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: The results on TH control of metamorphosis in Acanthurus triostegus are consistent with the model of metamorphosis in amphibians and other fish species.
source: These results are consistent with the model of metamorphosis in amphibians (Brown and Cai, 2007) and other fish species (McMenamin and Parichy, 2013).
evidence: Comparison to established models supported by citations to Brown and Cai, 2007 and McMenamin and Parichy, 2013.

claim: In both Acanthurus triostegus and zebrafish, as well as in flatfish, major pigmentation and craniofacial changes occur at metamorphosis.
source: Indeed, in both species, as well as in flatfish, another classical teleost model of metamorphosis, major pigmentation and craniofacial changes occur at metamorphosis (McMenamin and Parichy, 2013; McMenamin et al., 2014).
evidence: Comparison across species supported by citations to McMenamin and Parichy, 2013 and McMenamin et al., 2014.

claim: The onset and coordination of metamorphosis are two distinct events, both coordinated by TH and under environmental control.
source: Altogether, our findings indicate that the onset and coordination of metamorphosis are two distinct events, both coordinated by TH and under environmental control.
evidence: Inferred from combined experimental data on TH levels, TR expression, and environmental manipulation.

claim: Acanthurus triostegus larval recruitment is a TH-controlled metamorphosis, as in amphibians and flatfishes.
source: They further demonstrate that A. triostegus larval recruitment is a TH-controlled metamorphosis, as in amphibians and flatfishes (Brown and Cai, 2007; Laudet, 2011; McMenamin and Parichy, 2013).
evidence: Summary conclusion based on experimental data and comparison to other taxa, supported by citations to Brown and Cai, 2007; Laudet, 2011; McMenamin and Parichy, 2013.

claim: The decrease of both T4 and T3 after reef entry can be generalized to phylogenetically distant coral fish species.
source: We demonstrated that the decrease of both T4 and T3 after reef entry can be generalized to phylogenetically distant coral fish species (Figure 4).
evidence: Based on hormone measurements in four additional species shown in Figure 4.

claim: The decrease in TH levels after reef entry is valid for most if not all coral reef fishes, even if species-specific variations on this general theme can be observed.
source: We propose that this decrease is valid for most if not all coral reef fishes, even if species-specific variations on this general theme can be observed, and that the larval recruitment of coral reef fish corresponds to a TH-controlled metamorphosis (Figure 6A).
evidence: Generalization proposed based on data from five species, with acknowledgment of potential variation.

claim: Variations in the magnitude of TH changes among the five coral reef fish species are reminiscent of the situation in stickleback, where differences in TH signaling between two ecotypes support life history trait variation.
source: Interestingly, variations in the magnitude of TH changes among the five coral reef fish species (Figure 4) are reminiscent of the situation in stickleback, where differences in TH signaling between two ecotypes support life history trait variation (Kitano et al., 2010; Kitano and Lema, 2013).
evidence: Comparison to stickleback supported by citations to Kitano et al., 2010 and Kitano and Lema, 2013.

claim: This post-embryonic developmental step is shaped by evolution and varies according to species-specific life history traits such as pelagic larval duration, size at reef colonization and pigmentation status at recruitment.
source: We anticipate that this post-embryonic developmental step is shaped by evolution and varies according to species-specific life history traits such as pelagic larval duration, size at reef colonization and pigmentation status (i.e., metamorphic state of advancement) at recruitment.
evidence: Speculation based on observed variation among species and evolutionary reasoning.

claim: Coral reef fish could be excellent models to decipher how changes in life history strategies are elicited by changes in hormonal systems.
source: Given the dramatic diversity of life history strategies they propose, coral reef fish could be excellent models to decipher how these changes are elicited by changes in hormonal systems.
evidence: Speculation about future research potential based on observed diversity.

claim: CPF is known to be a thyroid disruptor with adverse effects on fish behavior.
source: Among the endocrine disruptors already evidenced and encountered in coral reefs, CPF is known to be a thyroid disruptor with adverse effects on fish behavior (Sandahl et al., 2005; Kavitha and Rao, 2008; Roche et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2011; Botté et al., 2012; Deb and Das, 2013; Juberg et al., 2013; Slotkin et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to Sandahl et al., 2005; Kavitha and Rao, 2008; Roche et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2011; Botté et al., 2012; Deb and Das, 2013; Juberg et al., 2013; Slotkin et al., 2013.

claim: CPF exposure reduces Acanthurus triostegus physiological level of T3 at larval recruitment.
source: We demonstrated that CPF exposure reduces A. triostegus physiological level of T3 at larval recruitment (Figure 5A).
evidence: Based on hormone measurement data from CPF exposure experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Exposure to CPF impairs metamorphosis in Acanthurus triostegus, as evidenced with the repression of guts' lengthening and the decrease in the juveniles' grazing activity.
source: Consistently with our observations on NH3 treated fish, exposure to CPF impairs metamorphosis, as evidenced with the repression of guts' lengthening (Figure 5B), and the decrease in the juveniles' grazing activity (Figure 5C).
evidence: Based on experimental data from CPF exposure experiments shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: CPF-induced reduction in grazing activity led to a reduced algal removal efficiency.
source: This latter point led to a reduced algal removal efficiency (Figure 5D).
evidence: Based on measurement of grazed algae biomass shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Acanthurus triostegus is one of the major herbivorous fish in coral reefs.
source: As A. triostegus is one of the major herbivorous fish in coral reefs, this can severely impair the ability of coral reefs to recover after an algal invasion (e.g., after a bleaching event) and therefore contributes to the worldwide degradation of reef health (Russ, 1984; Almany et al., 2007; Ledlie et al., 2007; Hughes et al., 2007; Hughes et al., 2014) (Figure 6B).
evidence: Stated as known fact and supported by citations to Russ, 1984; Almany et al., 2007; Ledlie et al., 2007; Hughes et al., 2007; Hughes et al., 2014.

claim: Impaired grazing by Acanthurus triostegus can severely impair the ability of coral reefs to recover after an algal invasion and therefore contributes to the worldwide degradation of reef health.
source: As A. triostegus is one of the major herbivorous fish in coral reefs, this can severely impair the ability of coral reefs to recover after an algal invasion (e.g., after a bleaching event) and therefore contributes to the worldwide degradation of reef health (Russ, 1984; Almany et al., 2007; Ledlie et al., 2007; Hughes et al., 2007; Hughes et al., 2014) (Figure 6B).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data on CPF effects on grazing, combined with knowledge about reef ecology supported by citations.

claim: Coral reef fish larval recruitment is a TH-regulated metamorphosis at the crossroads of ecological, developmental, physiological and behavioral transformations.
source: Our results highlight how coral reef fish larval recruitment, the transition between the open ocean and the reef, is a TH-regulated metamorphosis at the crossroads of ecological, developmental, physiological and behavioral transformations (Holzer and Laudet, 2015).
evidence: Summary conclusion based on all experimental findings, with citation to Holzer and Laudet, 2015.

claim: Coral reef fish TH signaling and larval recruitment processes can be altered by reef pollution.
source: These findings also demonstrate how coral reef fish TH signaling and larval recruitment processes can be altered by reef pollution.
evidence: Based on experimental data showing CPF effects on TH levels and metamorphosis.

claim: Metamorphosis and larval recruitment are essential for the maintenance of fish populations and subsequent coral reef resilience.
source: Since metamorphosis and larval recruitment are essential for the maintenance of fish populations and subsequent coral reef resilience, this study provides a general framework to better understand, at the molecular level, how global changes, water pollution and human activities can threaten reef ecosystems.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the conclusion.

claim: This study provides a general framework to better understand, at the molecular level, how global changes, water pollution and human activities can threaten reef ecosystems.
source: Since metamorphosis and larval recruitment are essential for the maintenance of fish populations and subsequent coral reef resilience, this study provides a general framework to better understand, at the molecular level, how global changes, water pollution and human activities can threaten reef ecosystems.
evidence: Summary statement of the study's broader implications based on all findings.

claim: IOP is used as an inhibitor of the deiodinase enzymes that prevents the degradation of injected T3.
source: T3 +iopanoic acid (IOP) both at 10−6 M, IOP being used as an inhibitor of the deiodinase enzymes that therefore prevents the degradation of injected T3 (Galton, 1989; Little et al., 2013; Lorgen et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to Galton, 1989; Little et al., 2013; Lorgen et al., 2015.

claim: NH3 is used as an antagonist of TR that prevents the binding of TH on TR.
source: NH3 at 10−6 M, NH3 being used as an antagonist of TR that prevents the binding of TH on TR (Lim et al., 2002; Renko et al., 2012) therefore disrupting A. triostegus TH pathway (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: Supported by citations to Lim et al., 2002 and Renko et al., 2012, and confirmed by transactivation assay data.

claim: Injections of T3 + IOP + NH3 result in an intestine length similar to the control individuals at day 2 and day 5, showing that T3 and NH3 effectively compete and confirming the non-toxicity of NH3.
source: Injections of T3 + IOP + NH3 result in an intestine length similar to the control individuals at day 2 and day 5 (p-values=0.486 and 0.444 respectively, Figure 3E). This shows that T3 and NH3 effectively compete, and confirms the non-toxicity of NH3.
evidence: Based on experimental data showing that combined treatment reverses the effects of T3 alone.

claim: Pigmentation during the larva to juvenile transition is strongly coupled to the environment but is not directly under TH control that may not sustain such rapid pigmentation changes.
source: This suggests that pigmentation during the larva to juvenile transition is strongly coupled to the environment but is not directly under TH control that may not sustain such rapid pigmentation changes.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that relocation affects pigmentation but TH/NH3 treatments do not.

claim: Intestine lengthening and remodeling are mediated by TH signaling in Acanthurus triostegus.
source: Taken together: (i) intestine lengthening and remodeling are mediated by TH signaling; and (ii) disturbing the TH pathway disrupts the normal development of fish after larval recruitment, showing that TH effectively controls some major aspects of A. triostegus metamorphosis.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on experimental manipulation data with TH agonists and antagonists.

claim: Disturbing the TH pathway disrupts the normal development of fish after larval recruitment, showing that TH effectively controls some major aspects of Acanthurus triostegus metamorphosis.
source: Taken together: (i) intestine lengthening and remodeling are mediated by TH signaling; and (ii) disturbing the TH pathway disrupts the normal development of fish after larval recruitment, showing that TH effectively controls some major aspects of A. triostegus metamorphosis.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on experimental manipulation data with TH agonists and antagonists.

claim: Acanthurus triostegus larvae start to graze a couple of days after colonizing the reef.
source: To achieve this, we used grazing activity (number of bites on algal turf), as A. triostegus larvae start to graze a couple of days after colonizing the reef, to investigate how TH signaling and metamorphosis completion influence the behavior of recruited fish.
evidence: Stated as observational fact used to justify the experimental approach.

claim: Acanthurus triostegus larvae do not feed for at least 12 hr after colonizing the reef at night.
source: Bite counting was not performed on crest captured individuals as A. triostegus larvae do not feed for at least 12 hr after colonizing the reef at night (MB pers. obs.).
evidence: Based on personal observation (MB pers. obs.).

claim: CPF is an agricultural insecticide that is widely used on tropical coastal crops, therefore one of the most common waterborne chemical pollutants encountered in coral reef surrounding waters.
source: Chlorpyrifos (CPF) is an agricultural insecticide that is widely used on tropical coastal crops, therefore one of the most common waterborne chemical pollutants encountered in coral reef surrounding waters (Cavanagh et al., 1999; Leong et al., 2007; Roche et al., 2011; Botté et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cavanagh et al., 1999; Leong et al., 2007; Roche et al., 2011; Botté et al., 2012.

claim: The exposure doses of CPF used (1, 5 or 30 µg.l−1 of seawater) were previously reported in coral reef fish.
source: To achieve this, we used exposure doses previously reported in coral reef fish (1, 5 or 30 µg.l−1 of seawater) (Botté et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Botté et al., 2012.

claim: No effect of CPF treatments on fish pigmentation was observed at day 2 and day 5.
source: We did not observe any effect of CPF treatments on fish pigmentation at day 2 and day 5 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Based on observational data shown in supplementary figure.

claim: The involvement of the TH signaling pathway in larval recruitment provides an entry point to study how anthropogenic stressors may affect reef fish populations.
source: The involvement of the TH signaling pathway in this key post-embryonic step, thus prone to endocrine disruption, provides an obvious entry point to study how anthropogenic stressors may affect reef fish populations.
evidence: Summary statement of the study's implications based on findings about TH control and CPF disruption.
